Every time we start or end a season of Elementary, my mind tends to turn to the same idea: what is this show about, exactly?

In season one, Elementary was a show about Joan Watson and Sherlock Holmes’ partnership, and the way their relationship helped each battle their respective demons. But with that relationship largely settled, the second and third seasons have struggled to find a dynamic resting rate for the series. There are serialized arcs that operate over top of the basic procedural dynamic, which are hit (Kitty) and miss (Mycroft), but that resting rate has been a problem as the third season came to a close. Although these are still fun characters to watch solve crimes, and there remains something inherently pleasurable about seeing a case start and end in the span of an hour, the show reached a point by the end of season three where the writers had run out of ways to draw conflict out of the show’s basic premise.

And so Sherlock relapses.

“A Controlled Descent” lives up to its title, I suppose: the show has had the relapse card in its pocket since the show began—as the “Previously On” sequence going back to the pilot reminds us—but has resisted playing it, at least until the writers found themselves needing a new element to mix things up. This season in particular, we saw the flashback to Sherlock’s moment in London where Kitty saved him from using, and the storyline with Oscar (Michael Weston) earlier in the season brought Sherlock’s past back to the surface. Although I would argue playing this card is a sign of desperation in a sense, the development was threaded throughout the season and the series, and developed in ways that felt both starkly honest to the reality of living in recovery and frustratingly contrary to the character we’ve thought we’ve known. It’s an easy card to play, but it’s played well.

Not anymore, but I used to be a professional pool player, and the cues I used (some I still have) ran anywhere from $600 - $20,000. I'm not sure how to justify a $20,000 stick over a $600 stick, but certainly anything less than $600 is probably not a very good cue.

What defines a good pool cue vs a bad one other then obvious things like being curved or having a tip that is carp/unreplaceable? I have only ever played for fun but know that some suck badly Just not sure with the difference is between that one is good ($50) and that is a pro pool cue ($600).

Mainly the quality of construction and the quality of materials. Generally the best cues are made from hard rock maple, seasoned, and treated. The best manufacturers take weeks and even months between lathe turnings in an effort to reduce warping. Any good stick will have a quality ferrule, and a laminated leather tip. you might ask, "what is the best cue?" Well, the best cue is the cue that works best for you. Some like Predator or Viking, some like Muecci or Schon. A lot depends on the feel for you. What you should stay away from is the cheap production cues, or the ones made from fiberglass or aluminum. If the top 18 inches or so of the shaft are varnished, this is a good sign it is a cheap cue.

Fancy doesn't necessarily mean good. All the extra stuff like inlays, wraps, rings, etc... all increase the price of a cue, but have no bearing on the quality of the cue. For many years I played with a $150 Dufferin Sneaky Pete, and won many a tournament with it. I also still have a Balabushka Original that's worth somewhere between $20,000 and $40,000 that plays like shit for me. And compared with the newer technology used by the likes of Predator, the Balabushka really is not a very good cue outside of a collectors item.

If you really want some in-depth info on cues and cue selection, shoot me a PM and we can talk about it.

FYI - IMHO the top cue mfgs:

Predator Muecci Schon McDermott Joss

Middle of the road:

Viking Lucasi Players Action

Any of these will make a decent cue, and unless you are really a player, you will not be able to discern a lot of difference other than the feel.

Somebody asked whether companies would be able to use litigation (or the threat of) to silence negative product reviews under the TPP.

A response given was:

No. From article 18.66: Each Party shall endeavour to achieve an appropriate balance in its copyright and related rights system ... [and give] due consideration to legitimate purposes such as ... criticism ...

The words chosen in this document are picked very deliberately. 'Shall endeavour' and even 'give due consideration' are specifically chosen to minimize the weight of said clauses and open the door for selective or non enforcement. Compare this, for instance, to:

Article 18.18 : Types of Signs Registrable as Trademarks No Party shall require, as a condition of registration, that a sign be visually perceptible, nor shall a Party deny registration of a trademark only on the ground that the sign of which it is composed is a sound.

This is an imperative. Though I've only read a tiny fraction of the text so far a recurring theme is for clauses that could actually help out society to be wrapped in these sort of 'shall endeavour' type phrasings. However, clauses the directly benefit corporations are instead generally stated as clear and mandatory imperatives.
